analysis.title: US midterms & data centres: slower build-out, cycle likely intact
key_insights: On 5 November the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) fell 12.3% as investors assessed the effect of Democratic election gains on the cost and pace of data centre expansion, amid local concern over electricity bills.

Syz's central case is a slower, more geographically dispersed AI data-centre build-out, partly outside the US. It reads the sell-off as a repricing of the AI trade, not of the broader economy, with no signs of stress in credit markets.
AI capital spending is still expected to reach USD 1.0tn in 2026 and USD 1.4tn in 2027. Some observers expect capex to peak as early as 2027, with up to a fifth of planned capacity at risk.

Democrats favouring tighter rules won governorships in Texas, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio, and local voters backed restrictions on new projects. Texas accounts for nearly 30% of US data centre capacity planned for 2028 (SemiAnalysis).
Both parties were wary: of 74 gubernatorial candidates, only 8 backed data centres outright, 40 called for regulation and 20 for a moratorium.

Grid spending is expected to continue. Texas has 474 GW of large-load connection requests, more than five times its record peak, and regulators approved two of the three import paths of the $33bn Permian Basin plan.

Delays raise the value of existing capacity. H100 rents are up about 35% since January and B200 rents have risen faster (Ornn Data via a16z), which lifts the value of deployed GPUs and powered sites and spreads hardware spending over more years.
SemiAnalysis forecasts about 38 GW of new US capacity in 2027, of which 22 GW was under vertical construction in September. It estimates moratoriums genuinely delay only about 2.3 GW.

After the 5 November drop the SOX is about 38% below its June peak but still up 28% this year. After the Nasdaq's seven previous one-day falls of more than 5% since 2015, it was lower a week later in five cases and higher three months later in six cases (small sample).

Syz treats local opposition as an added risk premium for AI infrastructure equities, not a reason to change its broader equity outlook. About 400 GW of US capacity is proposed against roughly 90 GW needed by 2030, so power, permits, financing and execution will separate winners from losers.

Most exposed: leveraged developers, companies relying on new approvals, and utilities facing a review of allowed returns. More resilient: hyperscalers and semiconductor suppliers backed by global AI demand. Potential beneficiaries: operators with secured power and permits, grid equipment suppliers, and utilities in states with stable frameworks.
Allianz Research counts nearly $200bn of projects blocked or delayed by local opposition in H1 2026, plus 261 local moratoria and 833 opposition groups across 49 states.

Texas: Governor Abbott ordered an audit of every data centre seeking a grid connection, the state environmental agency was told on 21 September to halt data-centre permits, and a review of a $3.3bn tax exemption is under way. Governor-elect Hinojosa (takes office 19 January) campaigned on a moratorium and ending tax breaks, but a Republican state Senate makes stricter cost-sharing more plausible than a permanent ban.

Georgia: Democrats now hold a 3-2 majority on the commission that sets the main utility's allowed returns, though the current rate agreement protects until 2028. Ohio voters backed bans aimed at specific hyperscaler campuses, and 21 local ballot measures were held. New York has a one-year moratorium on projects of 50 MW or more.

Syz sees the market possibly overpricing risk in AZ, FL, IA, KS, MI and WI because durable frameworks limit how far campaign rhetoric can travel. In Pennsylvania and Oregon the commission review of allowed returns matters more than the election.
What would change Syz's view: slowing AI revenue growth, weaker cloud utilisation, tighter financing for the largest platforms, or cuts to hyperscaler capex guidance. None are visible today.

sector_views.rationale: Balance sheets and geographic flexibility let them absorb delays.
Suppliers are supported by global AI demand, but the SOX fell 12.3% on 5 November and local opposition is an added risk premium for AI infrastructure.
Exposed where allowed returns are under review (Georgia, Pennsylvania, Oregon). Those in states with stable frameworks and grid modernisation are potential beneficiaries.
Grid reinvestment is accepted by both parties and continues regardless of who pays.
Most exposed to new approvals, moratoriums and tighter financing.

earnings_insights: Hyperscaler Q4 results and 2027 capex guidance in late January are flagged as the next checkpoint for the AI capex outlook.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Spending is still expected to reach this level despite the political backlash.
Most 2027 capacity is already under construction, which supports this figure.

risk_factors: Local moratoria, permit halts and cost-sharing rules in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and New York.
Tighter financing for the largest AI platforms would raise the probability of the capex-peak bear case.
Slowing AI revenue growth, weaker cloud utilisation, or cuts to hyperscaler capex guidance.
Utilities facing reviews of allowed returns, notably in Georgia, Pennsylvania and Oregon.
Low visibility until new governors and legislatures write rules in the first half of 2027.
vol_and_positioning: The SOX fell 12.3% on 5 November and sits about 38% below its June peak, still up 28% on the year. The Nasdaq has had seven one-day falls of more than 5% since 2015, and after each it was lower after one week in five cases and higher after three months in six.
geopolitical: US midterm and gubernatorial elections on 3 November brought data-centre opposition into governors' offices and utility commissions, with Democratic gains in Texas, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio.

tension_points.bull_case: Most 2027 capacity (22 GW of 38 GW) is already under construction, grid reinvestment is bipartisan, and H100 rents up about 35% show demand persists, so the cycle is delayed or relocated, not ended.
tension_points.bear_case: Moratoriums and the end of tax breaks could bring the capex peak forward to 2027, with up to 20% of planned AI data-centre capacity off the roadmap and debt-funded projects stalling.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Slowing AI revenue growth, weaker cloud utilisation, tighter financing for the largest platforms, or cuts to hyperscaler capex guidance (next checkpoint: late January Q4 results and 2027 capex guidance).

theme_stances.key_argument: Local opposition slows and disperses the build-out but the AI cycle stays intact because projects are under way and the grid must be rebuilt.
theme_stances.evidence: slower, more geographically dispersed build-out, partly outside the US
